fixes.explanation: That's right, baker. The text says, “And the people served the LORD throughout the days of Joshua…” (Judges 2:7). Joshua took over leading Israel after Moses died (Joshua 1:1–2). So picture a whole stretch of days with the people serving the LORD. I'd bake a double batch for a run like that.

Here's what the text says: “And the people served the LORD throughout the days of Joshua…” (Judges 2:7). Joshua led Israel after Moses died (Joshua 1:1–2). So through all his days, the people were serving the LORD. Enjoy this bright spot, because the story is about to turn.

Yes, friend. The text says the people served the LORD through the days of Joshua “…and of the elders who outlived him…” (Judges 2:7). The verse describes those elders as “…who had seen all the great works that the LORD had done for Israel.” So the serving lasted as long as the people who had seen those works. Keep that in your back pocket, because it matters in a few verses.

Gilgal doesn't show up in this passage, friend. The text says they buried Joshua “…in the land of his inheritance, at Timnath-heres in the hill country of Ephraim…” (Judges 2:9). I got stuffed in a junk drawer once, so a resting place with a full address, hill country and all, sounds mighty fancy to me. Joshua's is Timnath-heres.

Yes. The text says “…another generation rose up who did not know the LORD or the works that He had done for Israel.” (Judges 2:10). Compare the elders, who “…had seen all the great works that the LORD had done for Israel.” (Judges 2:7). Different generation, different knowing. I think that's a big gap to fall into.

Yes, baker. The text says they “…followed after various gods of the peoples around them.” (Judges 2:12). Notice the word various, because it wasn't just one god. And this is in the same verse that reminds us the LORD brought their fathers out of Egypt.

It goes the other way, friend. The text says the LORD “…sold them into the hands of their enemies all around, whom they were no longer able to resist.” (Judges 2:14). Driving enemies out isn't what the verse describes. It describes Israel no longer able to resist them.

Yes, friend. The text says, “Wherever Israel marched out, the hand of the LORD was against them to bring calamity…” (Judges 2:15). Calamity is the verse's own word. I think this is a heavy one to read.

Victory is what you'd hope for when marching out, friend. But the text says the hand of the LORD was against them “…to bring calamity…” (Judges 2:15). Calamity is the word the verse uses. Nobody packs a lunch for that kind of march.

The text says otherwise, friend. The hand of the LORD was against them to bring calamity, “…just as He had sworn to them.” (Judges 2:15). The calamity matched what He had sworn. So True is the one that fits the verse.

Shiloh isn't in this passage, baker. The text says the LORD “…raised up judges, who saved them from the hands of those who plundered them.” (Judges 2:16). These judges are rescuers, not worship leaders. Israel is plundered in verse 14, and by verse 16 the LORD raises up judges. That's a quick turn in the story.

The neighbors' gods do come up in this story, friend (Judges 2:12). But this verse is about the way of their fathers, “…who had walked in obedience to the LORD’s commandments…” (Judges 2:17). The text says Israel quickly turned from that way. So the word you want is fathers.

Altars would be a fair guess, baker, but the verse uses a different word. The LORD says, “I will no longer drive out before them any of the nations Joshua left when he died.” (Judges 2:21). Nations, meaning peoples still in the land. I've reached for the raisins when I wanted the chocolate chips plenty of times, so no shame here.

Yes, baker. The text says, “And they took the daughters of these people in marriage, gave their own daughters to their sons, and served their gods.” (Judges 3:6). Marriages in both directions, and serving their gods, all in one verse. That's a lot packed into a single line.
